title: A page with no identity
summary: Repair the storefront HTML so its structure communicates meaning to browsers and assistive technology.

scenario.briefing: The storefront renders as a wall of text. Screen readers cannot find headings or navigation, and product cards are anonymous divs. Rebuild the structure without changing the content.

objectives.description: Give the page a header, navigation, main content, and articles.
Provide meaningful alternative text and labeled actions.
Check understanding through the remaining explanation and transfer evidence.

hints: Start with header, nav, main, and article instead of div elements.
Each product can be an article with class product. Add one h1 for the store name.
Images need alt text. Buttons need a data-action attribute for the order logic.
Use header h1 Campus store, nav with three links, two article.product blocks, images with alt text, and buttons with data-action="add".

misconceptions.description: Treating visual layout as sufficient structure.
misconceptions.testDescription: The page has a main landmark.
misconceptions.feedback: Styling cannot tell assistive technology what a region means. Use header, nav, main, and article elements.
Every meaningful image needs alt text describing its purpose. Decorative images use an empty alt, but product images carry information.

misconceptions.description: Believing CSS can supply document structure for assistive technology.
misconceptions.feedback: CSS controls presentation. Roles and text alternatives must exist in the HTML for assistive technology to expose them.

sections.title: HTML describes meaning
sections.body: HTML elements name the role of content: header for introductory material, nav for navigation, main for the page's central content, article for a self-contained item. Browsers and assistive technology use these roles.

sections.title: Structure is not appearance
sections.body: CSS decides how the page looks. HTML decides what the content is. A page made entirely of div elements can look fine and still be difficult to navigate with a keyboard or screen reader.

vocabulary.definition: An element whose name describes meaning, such as nav or article.
A text description of an image for people who cannot see it.
A region assistive technology can jump to, such as main or nav.

hints: Replace the generic containers with landmarks and product articles, and give each image a real text alternative.
HTML elements carry roles: header, nav, main, and article tell assistive technology what each region is.
A page with a top heading and two products needs a header with an h1, a nav with links, a main, and two articles.

Start from the body: make the brand an h1 inside header, wrap the links in nav, put the content in main, convert each product div to article.product, add alt text, and mark both add buttons with data-action="add".
steps.title: Repair the storefront structure
steps.prompt: Edit index.html. Use header, nav, main, article.product, and meaningful controls. Run the structure tests when done. CSS is provided and should not need changes.

tests.description: A header landmark contains the store heading.
The page has a main landmark.
Both products are articles with the product class.
Both add buttons expose the add action.

hints: Select statements about the relationship between structure and presentation.
Semantic HTML communicates roles; CSS only changes appearance.
A screen reader can jump to a main landmark even when the page looks identical without CSS.
Two statements are accurate; reject CSS-as-structure and the absolute claim that div is never valid.
steps.title: Structure and appearance

statements.label: HTML elements communicate roles to browsers and assistive technology.
CSS alone can replace missing document structure for screen readers.
A div can never be part of a correct page.

steps.explanation: Semantic elements and text alternatives carry meaning. Div elements are appropriate for generic grouping, but not as a substitute for every meaningful role.
